items.stem: Match the climatic factors with their effects : Column A Column B (1) Latitude (a) Brings wet air to India during summer (2) Altitude (b) Creates different climates in the north and south (3) Proximity to the ocean (c) Keeps higher places cooler (4) Monsoon winds (d) Moderates the temperature
items.answer:  (1) Latitude --- (b) Creates different climates in the north and south (2) Altitude --- (c) Keeps higher places cooler (3) Proximity to the ocean --- (d) Moderates the temperature (4) Monsoon winds --- (a) Brings wet air to India during summer

items.stem: Identify a natural disaster (e.g., cyclone, flood, landslide, or forest fire) and write a short essay that includes the causes and impacts. Suggest actions that individuals, communities and the government can take to reduce the impact.

items.stem: Traditionally, how many seasons or ‘ritus’ is the year divided into in many parts of India?

options.label: A
options.text: Three seasons

options.label: B
options.text: Four seasons

options.label: C
options.text: Five seasons

options.label: D
options.text: Six seasons

items.answer:  (D) Six seasons In many parts of India, the year is traditionally divided into six seasons or ‘ritus’ : Vasanta (spring), Grishma (summer), Varsha (rainy season), Sharad (autumn), Hemanta (pre-winter), and Shishir (winter), each with associated festivals.

items.stem: How are seasons primarily caused on Earth?

options.label: A
options.text: By the Earth’s daily rotation on axis

options.label: B
options.text: By the Earth’s revolution around the Sun

options.label: C
options.text: By changes in the Moon’s gravitational pull

options.label: D
options.text: By fluctuations in solar flare activity

items.answer:  (B) By the Earth’s revolution around the Sun Seasons occur due to the Earth’s revolution around the Sun and the tilt of its axis. This causes different parts of the Earth to receive more direct sunlight at different times of the year.

items.stem: What does an ‘alpine climate’, typically found in the Himalayan mountains, primarily feature? year

options.label: A
options.text: Hot, humid summers and very mild winters

options.label: B
options.text: Cold, snowy winters and very cool summers

options.label: C
options.text: Dry, arid conditions throughout the entire

options.label: D
options.text: Moderate rainfall and consistent temperatures

items.answer:  (B) Cold, snowy winters and very cool summers An alpine climate, characteristic of high mountain regions like the Himalayas, is defined by cold, snowy winters and cool summers. The term “alpine” is derived from the Alps mountain range in Europe.

items.stem: In which geographical region of India is a ‘subtropical’ climate with very hot summers and cold winters predominantly found?

options.label: A
options.text: The western coastal strip along Arabian Sea

options.label: B
options.text: The northern plains where wheat is grown

options.label: C
options.text: The central Deccan Plateau region of India

options.label: D
options.text: The Himalayan mountain range in north

items.answer:  (B) The northern plains where wheat is grown The northern plains of India experience a subtropical climate, characterized by very hot summers and distinct, cold winters. This climatic condition is suitable for growing crops like wheat, which is a staple here.

items.stem: How does an ‘arid climate’ like in the Thar Desert differ from a ‘tropical wet climate’ on the western coast?

options.label: A
options.text: Arid has heavy rain; tropical wet is dry

options.label: B
options.text: Arid has cool days; tropical wet has hot

options.label: C
options.text: Arid has little rain; tropical wet has much

options.label: D
options.text: Arid has mild winter; tropical wet has cold

items.answer:  (C) Arid has little rain; tropical wet has much An arid climate, found in the Thar Desert, features extremely little rainfall and hot days. In contrast, a tropical wet climate, like on the western coast, receives heavy rainfall, especially during monsoon months.

items.stem: Why are places near the Equator generally warmer than places near the poles? Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

options.label: A
options.text: The Equator is closer to the Sun

options.label: B
options.text: The Equator receives more direct sun rays

options.label: C
options.text: Polar regions have more cloud cover

options.label: D
options.text: Polar regions reflect more sunlight back

items.answer:  (B) The Equator receives more direct sun rays Equatorial regions are warmer because the sun’s rays strike the Earth’s surface at a more direct, perpendicular angle, concentrating solar energy over a smaller area. Near the poles, rays are oblique, spreading energy thinly.

items.stem: As altitude increases, what generally happens to the atmospheric temperature?

options.label: A
options.text: It increases rapidly

options.label: B
options.text: It decreases steadily

options.label: C
options.text: It remains constant

options.label: D
options.text: It fluctuates wildly

items.answer:  (B) It decreases steadily Temperature generally decreases with an increase in altitude. This is because the air becomes less dense at higher altitudes, and the Earth’s surface, which absorbs and radiates heat, is further away from there.

items.stem: Udhagamandalam (Ooty) and Coimbatore are at similar latitudes, but Ooty has cooler summers (10-25°C) than Coimbatore (25-38°C). What is the primary reason for this temperature difference?

options.label: A
options.text: Ooty is closer to the sea moderators

options.label: B
options.text: Coimbatore receives less annual rainfall yearly

options.label: C
options.text: Ooty is located at a higher altitude

options.label: D
options.text: Coimbatore has more industrial activity

items.answer:  (C) Ooty is located at a higher altitude Ooty’s cooler temperatures compared to Coimbatore, despite similar latitudes, are primarily due to its higher altitude. Temperature generally decreases with increasing elevation, making hill stations like Ooty cooler than nearby plains.

items.stem: Why do coastal areas generally experience more moderate temperatures (less extreme summers and winters) compared to inland areas?

options.label: A
options.text: Coastal areas have more vegetation

options.label: B
options.text: Inland areas receive more direct sunlight

options.label: C
options.text: The sea acts as a temperature moderator

options.label: D
options.text: Winds are stronger in coastal regions

items.answer:  (C) The sea acts as a temperature moderator The sea absorbs and releases heat more slowly than land. This moderating effect means coastal areas don’t get as hot in summer or as cold in winter as inland areas, resulting in a smaller temperature range.

items.stem: Winds blowing from the deserts of Arabia to Afghanistan often bring dry and hot air to states like Punjab and Haryana, causing severe _____ in summer.

options.label: A
options.text: floods

options.label: B
options.text: snowfalls

options.label: C
options.text: heat waves

options.label: D
options.text: cyclones

items.answer:  (C) heat waves Winds originating from hot desert regions, like those from Arabia, carry dry and intensely hot air. When these winds reach northwestern India, they can cause severe heat waves during the summer months in that region.

items.stem: What does ‘topography’ refer to in the context of factors determining climate?

options.label: A
options.text: The types of soil found in a region

options.label: B
options.text: The physical surface features of an area

options.label: C
options.text: The amount of pollution in atmosphere

options.label: D
options.text: The density of human population nearby

items.answer:  (B) The physical surface features of an area Topography refers to the arrangement of the natural and artificial physical features of an area. This includes mountains, hills, valleys, plains, and slopes, all of which can significantly influence local and regional climates.

items.stem: How do the Himalayas primarily affect India’s climate regarding winds from Central Asia?

options.label: A
options.text: They channel cold winds into India mostly

options.label: B
options.text: They act as a barrier against cold winds

options.label: C
options.text: They generate warm winds that blow south

options.label: D
options.text: They have no significant impact on winds

items.answer:  (B) They act as a barrier against cold winds The Himalayan mountain range acts as a formidable barrier, protecting the Indian subcontinent to a large extent from the extremely cold, dry winds blowing from the cold deserts of Central Asia during winter.

items.stem: What is a ‘microclimate’? NODIA CH 03: Climates of India

options.label: A
options.text: The climate of a very large continent

options.label: B
options.text: A climate localized in a small area

options.label: C
options.text: The historical climate of an ancient city

options.label: D
options.text: A climate predicted by computer models

items.answer:  (B) A climate localized in a small area A microclimate refers to the specific climatic conditions in a very small or restricted area that differ from the climate of the surrounding region. Enclosed valleys or urban areas can develop their own microclimates.

items.stem: The word ‘monsoon’ comes from the Arabic word ‘mausim’. What does ‘mausim’ mean?

options.label: A
options.text: Rain

options.label: B
options.text: Wind

options.label: C
options.text: Season

options.label: D
options.text: Storm

items.answer:  (C) Season The term ‘monsoon’ originates from the Arabic word ‘mausim,’ which means ‘season.’ It refers to the seasonal reversal of wind patterns, which brings distinct wet and dry periods to large regions, notably South Asia.

items.stem: During the summer monsoon in India, winds are drawn from the cooler, high-pressure ocean towards the hot, low-pressure landmass. What do these ocean winds primarily carry?

options.label: A
options.text: Dry desert air

options.label: B
options.text: Cold polar air

options.label: C
options.text: Volcanic ash

options.label: D
options.text: Moisture for rain

items.answer:  (D) Moisture for rain As winds blow from the relatively cooler ocean (high pressure) towards the heated Asian landmass (low pressure) during summer, they pick up significant amounts of moisture. This moisture condenses over land, resulting in heavy monsoon rains.

items.stem: How does the Northeast Monsoon (winter monsoon) generally differ from the Southwest Monsoon (summer monsoon) in terms of conditions it brings to much of Asia? cold

options.label: A
options.text: Northeast brings heavy rain; Southwest is dry

options.label: B
options.text: Northeast brings dry; Southwest brings rain

options.label: C
options.text: Both bring similar amounts of the rainfall

options.label: D
options.text: Northeast brings warm; Southwest brings

items.answer:  (B) Northeast brings dry; Southwest brings rain The Southwest Monsoon brings moisture-laden winds from the ocean to the land, causing widespread rain. The Northeast Monsoon involves winds blowing from the cooler landmass towards the ocean, generally bringing dry conditions to much of Asia.

items.stem: Mawsynram, located in Meghalaya, holds what distinction regarding rainfall?

options.label: A
options.text: It receives the lowest average annual rainfall

options.label: B
options.text: It receives the highest average annual rainfall

options.label: C
options.text: It experiences rainfall only in winter month

options.label: D
options.text: It has never recorded any snowfall

items.answer:  (B) It receives the highest average annual rainfall Mawsynram in Meghalaya is renowned for receiving the highest average annual rainfall in the world, approximately 11,000 mm (11 meters). This extreme precipitation is due to its unique topographical location and monsoon patterns.

items.stem: Which of the following pairs correctly matches a traditional Indian season (ritu) with its approximate English equivalent?

options.label: A
options.text: Vasanta - Rainy Season

options.label: B
options.text: Grishma - Winter

options.label: C
options.text: Varsha - Summer

options.label: D
options.text: Sharad - Autumn

items.answer:  (D) Sharad - Autumn In the traditional Indian calendar, Sharad Ritu corresponds to the autumn season. Vasanta is spring, Grishma is summer, and Varsha is the rainy season, each with unique characteristics and cultural associations in India. Downloaded from www.pdf.tube

items.stem: What is a ‘cyclone’ in meteorological terms?

options.label: A
options.text: A prolonged period of very little rainfall

options.label: B
options.text: An intense low-pressure system with winds

options.label: C
options.text: A sudden, rapid melting of mountain glaciers

options.label: D
options.text: A fire spreading uncontrollably through forest

items.answer:  (B) An intense low-pressure system with winds A cyclone is a large-scale air mass that rotates around a strong center of low atmospheric pressure. It is characterized by inward spiraling winds that rotate counterclockwise (in the Northern Hemisphere) and often brings severe weather.

items.stem: What is the ‘eye of the cyclone’?

options.label: A
options.text: The outermost band of storm clouds

options.label: B
options.text: The point where the cyclone makes landfall

options.label: C
options.text: The calm, cloudless center of depression

options.label: D
options.text: The area with the heaviest rainfall mostly

items.answer:  (C) The calm, cloudless center of depression The ‘eye’ is the relatively calm, often clear, and warm central area of a strong tropical cyclone. It is surrounded by the eyewall, a ring of towering thunderstorms where the most severe weather occurs.

items.stem: Which organization in India is primarily responsible for tracking cyclones and providing information on their formation and movement?

options.label: A
options.text: National Disaster Response Force (NDRF)

options.label: B
options.text: Central Water Commission (CWC) of India

options.label: C
options.text: India Meteorological Department (IMD)

options.label: D
options.text: Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)

items.answer:  (C) India Meteorological Department (IMD) The India Meteorological Department (IMD) is the principal government agency responsible for meteorological observations, weather forecasting, and seismology, including the crucial task of tracking cyclones and issuing warnings for public safety.

items.stem: What is a ‘glacial burst’ or Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF)?

options.label: A
options.text: A sudden increase in glacier’s movement

options.label: B
options.text: The formation of new glaciers in winter

options.label: C
options.text: A sudden release of water from lake

options.label: D
options.text: The slow melting of a glacier’s snout

items.answer:  (C) A sudden release of water from lake A glacial burst, or GLOF, occurs when a dam containing a glacial lake fails, leading to a sudden and often catastrophic release of water. These events can cause devastating floods downstream in regions.

items.stem: Why might urban areas with extensive concrete surfaces experience flooding even with moderate rainfall?

options.label: A
options.text: Concrete absorbs too much water quickly

options.label: B
options.text: Concrete surfaces prevent water from soaking

options.label: C
options.text: Urban areas are built on floodplains

options.label: D
options.text: Tall buildings attract more rainfall

items.answer:  (B) Concrete surfaces prevent water from soaking Concrete and asphalt surfaces in urban areas are impermeable, meaning they do not allow rainwater to soak into the ground. This increases surface runoff, which can overwhelm drainage systems and lead to flooding.

items.stem: The National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) is specially trained to respond to what types of disasters?

options.label: A
options.text: Only earthquakes and tsunamis in world

options.label: B
options.text: Primarily financial and economic crises

options.label: C
options.text: Natural as well as human-made disasters

options.label: D
options.text: Only disasters occurring in urban areas

items.answer:  (C) Natural as well as human-made disasters The NDRF is a specialized force constituted for responding to a threatening disaster situation or disaster, whether natural (like cyclones, floods) or human-made (like industrial accidents), providing rescue and relief operations across India. NODIA CH 03: Climates of India

items.stem: What does “climate change” refer to in a broad sense? conditions rain

options.label: A
options.text: The daily fluctuations in local weather

options.label: B
options.text: Significant, long-term changes in the climate

options.label: C
options.text: The seasonal variations in temperature or

options.label: D
options.text: Efforts to predict next week’s forecast

items.answer:  (B) Significant, long-term changes in the climate Climate change refers to long-term shifts in temperatures and weather patterns. These shifts may be natural, but since the 1800s, human activities have been the main driver of climate change, primarily due to burning fossil fuels.

items.stem: How does the burning of fossil fuels primarily contribute to global warming and climate change?

options.label: A
options.text: It releases large amounts of oxygen

options.label: B
options.text: It depletes the Earth’s ozone layer

options.label: C
options.text: It releases excess greenhouse gases in air

options.label: D
options.text: It directly heats the Earth’s solid core

items.answer:  (C) It releases excess greenhouse gases in air Burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, and gas) releases large quantities of greenhouse gases, like carbon dioxide (CO2), into the atmosphere. These gases trap extra heat, enhancing the natural greenhouse effect and causing rapid global warming.

items.stem: The capacity to withstand or recover quickly from difficulties, such as climate-related disasters, is known as _____.

options.label: A
options.text: mitigation

options.label: B
options.text: adaptation

options.label: C
options.text: resilience

options.label: D
options.text: sustainability

items.answer:  (C) resilience Resilience refers to the ability of individuals, communities, or systems to withstand, adapt to, and recover quickly from shocks and stresses, such as those caused by climate change and associated natural disasters over time.

items.stem: A coastal community is experiencing rising sea levels and more frequent, intense storms. To cope, they are building sea walls and elevating homes. This process of adjusting to actual or expected climate and its effects is best termed as :

options.label: A
options.text: Climate mitigation effort

options.label: B
options.text: Climate adaptation strategy

options.label: C
options.text: Climate geoengineering project

options.label: D
options.text: Climate forecasting model

items.answer:  (B) Climate adaptation strategy Adaptation involves adjusting to the current and future effects of climate change. Building sea walls and elevating homes are strategies to reduce vulnerability and increase resilience to impacts like rising sea levels and stronger storms.

items.stem: Which pairing of a climate type found in India and its general characteristic is INCORRECT? winters and cool summers days, very little rainfall winters, moderate summer rain summers, moderate monsoon rainfall

options.label: A
options.text: Alpine Climate (Himalayas) - Cold, snowy

options.label: B
options.text: Arid Climate (Thar Desert) - Extremely hot

options.label: C
options.text: Tropical Wet Climate (Western Coast) - Dry

options.label: D
options.text: Semi-arid Climate (Deccan Plateau) - Hot

items.answer:  (C) Tropical Wet Climate (Western Coast) - Dry winters, moderate summer rain A tropical wet climate, like that on India’s western coast, is characterized by heavy rainfall, especially during the monsoon months, and typically does not have dry winters with only moderate summer rain as the primary characteristic.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : Mumbai, being near the sea, has cooler summers and milder winters than Nagpur, which is inland. Reason (R) : The sea absorbs and releases heat more slowly than land, moderating coastal temperatures. explanation of A. correct explanation of A.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer:  (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Coastal areas like Mumbai experience a moderating effect from the sea, which heats and cools slower than land. This results in less extreme temperatures (cooler summers, milder winters) compared to inland cities like Nagpur at similar latitudes. Click Here to Buy book on Flipkart

items.stem: The Western Ghats act as a barrier, affecting rainfall distribution. Which of the above statements is/are correct?

options.label: A
options.text: 1 and 3 only

options.label: B
options.text: 2 only

options.label: C
options.text: 1 and 2 only

options.label: D
options.text: 1, 2 and 3

items.answer:  (A) 1 and 3 only The Southwest monsoon brings summer rains advancing from south to north. The Northeast monsoon primarily brings rain to parts of the east and south coast. The Western Ghats significantly influence rainfall patterns, causing heavy rain on western slopes.

items.stem: What are “fossil fuels”? matter remains synthesis

options.label: A
options.text: Fuels derived from recently living plant

options.label: B
options.text: Energy sources formed from ancient organic

options.label: C
options.text: Fuels created through artificial chemical

options.label: D
options.text: Renewable energy sources like solar or wind

items.answer:  (B) Energy sources formed from ancient organic remains Fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) are energy sources formed over millions of years from the fossilized remains of ancient plants and animals buried under layers of sediment and subjected to heat and pressure.

items.stem: Which traditional Indian ritu (season) is associated with pre-winter?

options.label: A
options.text: Grishma

options.label: B
options.text: Varsha

options.label: C
options.text: Hemanta

options.label: D
options.text: Shishir

items.answer:  (C) Hemanta Hemanta is one of the six traditional Indian ritus and corresponds to the pre-winter season. This period typically follows autumn (Sharad) and precedes the peak winter season (Shishir) in many parts of India.

items.stem: Why are “urban heat islands” often warmer than their surrounding rural areas? absorbing

options.label: A
options.text: Rural areas have more sources of pollution

options.label: B
options.text: Urban areas have more reflective surfaces

options.label: C
options.text: Cities have less vegetation and more heat-

options.label: D
options.text: Rural areas experience stronger wind patterns

items.answer:  (C) Cities have less vegetation and more heat- absorbing Urban heat islands occur because cities typically have fewer trees and green spaces, and more buildings and concrete surfaces that absorb and retain solar radiation. Waste heat from human activities also contributes to higher temperatures.

items.stem: If fishermen on the Konkan coast observe fish that normally stay deep underwater appearing at the surface, what might this traditionally indicate about the weather?

options.label: A
options.text: The onset of a prolonged dry spell soon

options.label: B
options.text: The arrival of the monsoon season

options.label: C
options.text: An impending period of unusually cold

options.label: D
options.text: The likelihood of a severe dust storm

items.answer:  (B) The arrival of the monsoon season According to traditional knowledge in some coastal areas like the Konkan coast, certain changes in fish behavior, such as deep-water fish surfacing, are interpreted as signs of the approaching monsoon season and associated weather changes.

items.stem: How does latitude affect the amount of solar radiation received at a location on Earth? solar radiation atmosphere

options.label: A
options.text: Higher latitudes receive more concentrated

options.label: B
options.text: Lower latitudes receive less direct solar energy

options.label: C
options.text: Higher latitudes have sun rays pass more

options.label: D
options.text: Latitude has no significant effect on radiation

items.answer:  (C) Higher latitudes have sun rays pass more atmosphere At higher latitudes (near poles), sunlight strikes the Earth at an oblique angle, spreading the energy over a larger area and passing through more atmosphere, which reduces its intensity compared to lower latitudes (near Equator). NODIA CH 03: Climates of India

items.stem: Which of the following correctly pairs a type of climate disaster with its primary characteristic? area vegetation

options.label: A
options.text: Cyclone - Sudden collapse of rock and soil

options.label: B
options.text: Flood - Uncontrolled fire spreading through

options.label: C
options.text: Landslide - Overflow of water into dry land

options.label: D
options.text: Forest Fire - Uncontrolled burning of

items.answer:  (D) Forest Fire - Uncontrolled burning of vegetation A forest fire is an uncontrolled fire that spreads rapidly through vegetation like forests or grasslands. Cyclones involve strong winds, floods are water overflow, and landslides are sudden collapses of earth material on slopes.

items.stem: In the context of climate change, _____ refers to adopting steps to slow down global warming and reduce its causes.

options.label: A
options.text: resilience

options.label: B
options.text: adaptation

options.label: C
options.text: mitigation

options.label: D
options.text: sustainability

items.answer:  (C) mitigation Mitigation in the context of climate change involves actions aimed at reducing the emission of greenhouse gases or enhancing their removal from the atmosphere, thereby slowing down the rate of global warming and its causes.

items.stem: The phrase “monsoon failure” typically refers to what situation regarding rainfall?

options.label: A
options.text: Excessive and continuous rainfall over weeks

options.label: B
options.text: Rainfall occurring much earlier than expected

options.label: C
options.text: Poor or insufficient rainfall during monsoon

options.label: D
options.text: Rainfall that is too acidic for crops

items.answer:  (C) Poor or insufficient rainfall during monsoon “Monsoon failure” describes a situation where the monsoon season brings significantly less rainfall than average or expected. This can lead to drought, agricultural losses, and water scarcity in affected regions of India.

items.stem: What is the significance of the Subhashita “kale varshatu parjanyaha prithivi sasyashalini”.

options.label: A
options.text: It is a weather forecasting technique used

options.label: B
options.text: It is a prayer for timely rains, prosperity

options.label: C
options.text: It describes the scientific causes of climate

options.label: D
options.text: It is a historical record of past droughts

items.answer:  (B) It is a prayer for timely rains, prosperity This Subhashita is an ancient Sanskrit verse that expresses a wish or prayer for timely rainfall (“kale varshatu parjanyaha”) so that the Earth may be lush with vegetation (“prithivi sasyashalini”), signifying prosperity and well-being.

items.stem: All of the following are major factors determining the climate of a region EXCEPT :

options.label: A
options.text: The longitude of the place specifically

options.label: B
options.text: The altitude of the place

options.label: C
options.text: The region’s proximity to large seas

options.label: D
options.text: The prevailing wind patterns

items.answer:  (A) The longitude of the place specifically While latitude (distance from the Equator) is a major climate determinant, longitude (east-west position) by itself does not directly determine a region’s climate. Altitude, proximity to sea, and winds are significant influencing factors.

items.stem: A farmer in the Deccan Plateau relies heavily on monsoon rains for cultivating crops. If the India Meteorological Department predicts a ‘monsoon failure’ with below-average rainfall for the upcoming season, what is a likely challenge this farmer will face? excess heavy rain yield

options.label: A
options.text: Waterlogging and damage to crops due to

options.label: B
options.text: Difficulty in harvesting due to continuous

options.label: C
options.text: Water scarcity for irrigation, leading to poor

options.label: D
options.text: An unusually early onset of the winter season

items.answer:  (C) Water scarcity for irrigation, leading to poor yield A ‘monsoon failure’ implies insufficient rainfall. For a farmer in a region like the Deccan Plateau dependent on monsoons, this would lead to water scarcity for irrigating crops, likely resulting in reduced crop yields and economic hardship.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about India’s diverse climates contains an INCORRECT characteristic? lower hilly areas hot days NODIA heavy year-round rain distinct wet and dry

options.label: A
options.text: Himalayan mountains : Temperate climate in

options.label: B
options.text: Thar Desert : Arid climate with extremely

options.label: C
options.text: Northern Plains : Tropical wet climate with

options.label: D
options.text: Southern Peninsula : Tropical climate with

items.answer:  (C) Northern Plains : Tropical wet climate with heavy year-round rain The Northern Plains generally have a subtropical climate with very hot summers and cold winters, and monsoon rainfall, not a tropical wet climate with heavy year-round rain. The other descriptions are broadly accurate for those regions.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : Human activities since the 19th century have been the main driver of recent climate change. Reason (R) : The burning of fossil fuels and deforestation have significantly increased greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. explanation of A. correct explanation of A.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct

options.label: B

items.stem: Explain the key difference between weather and climate.
items.answer:  Weather refers to the atmospheric conditions (like rain, sun, wind) experienced hour-to-hour or day-to-day, while climate is the average weather pattern observed over a long period (decades).

items.stem: How are seasons related to both weather and climate?
items.answer:  Weather changes significantly with each season (e.g., hot summer, rainy monsoon). The regular pattern of these seasons occurring year after year defines the climate of a region.

items.stem: Describe the characteristics of an alpine climate found in the Himalayas.
items.answer:  An alpine climate features cold, snowy winters and cool summers. It is typical of high mountain regions, similar to the Alps in Europe, hence the name.

items.stem: Why are many ‘hill stations’ found in areas with a temperate climate?

items.stem: Briefly explain the arid climate of the Thar Desert.
items.answer:  The Thar Desert’s arid climate is characterized by extremely hot daytime temperatures, cool nights, and very scarce rainfall, requiring unique water conservation methods.

items.stem: How does latitude affect the temperature of a place?
items.answer:  Places near the Equator (low latitudes) receive direct sunlight focused on a small area, making them warmer. Places near the poles (high latitudes) receive slanted rays spread over a larger area, making them colder.

items.stem: Give one reason why temperature decreases with increasing altitude.
items.answer:  As altitude increases, air pressure and density decrease, causing the air to cool. Also, being farther from the Earth’s heated surface contributes to lower temperatures higher up.

items.stem: How does proximity to the sea moderate the temperature of coastal areas?
items.answer:  The sea heats up and cools down slower than land. In summer, cooler sea breezes moderate land temperature; in winter, the warmer sea air prevents extreme cold, resulting in milder temperatures year-round.

items.stem: Explain how winds blowing from the west affect North India’s weather in summer and winter.
items.answer:  In summer, westerly winds bring hot, dry air from deserts, causing heat waves. In winter, cold winds from across the Himalayas can creep in, causing cold waves in the foothills and plains.

items.stem: How does topography, like the Himalayas, influence India’s climate?
items.answer:  The Himalayas act as a barrier, partially protecting India from cold Central Asian winds. Mountain ranges also influence rainfall patterns by blocking moisture-laden winds (like the Western Ghats during monsoon).

items.stem: What is a microclimate? Give an example.
items.answer:  A microclimate is the distinct climate of a very small, localized area that differs from its surroundings. Examples include enclosed valleys, specific forest areas, or urban heat islands in cities.

items.stem: Briefly explain the basic mechanism that drives monsoon winds.
items.answer:  Land heats and cools faster than oceans. In summer, hot land creates low pressure, drawing moist winds from the high-pressure ocean. In winter, cooler land creates high pressure, pushing dry winds towards the lower-pressure ocean.

items.stem: Differentiate between the Southwest (summer) and Northeast (winter) monsoons in India.
items.answer:  The Southwest monsoon (June-July) brings moisture-laden winds from the ocean to the land, causing widespread heavy rain. The Northeast monsoon (winter) involves dry winds blowing from land to sea, bringing rain mainly to parts of the east coast after picking up moisture over the Bay of Bengal.

items.stem: How does traditional knowledge help in predicting monsoons? Give one example.
items.answer:  Generations of observation led to local indicators. For example, fishermen on the Konkan coast predict monsoon onset when deep-sea fish surface, or the flowering of the Golden Shower tree signals impending rain in some regions.

items.stem: Explain the term ‘monsoon failure’ and its immediate impact on people.
items.answer:  ‘Monsoon failure’ refers to significantly less rainfall than expected during the monsoon season. This severely affects agriculture, leads to water scarcity (forcing women to walk farther for water), and can cause migration of labourers. Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

items.stem: How is a cyclone formed.
items.answer:  Cyclones form over warm seas when intense low atmospheric pressure develops. Air from surrounding higher-pressure areas rushes in, bringing moisture, forming rotating clouds that spiral inwards towards the low-pressure centre (eye).

items.stem: What are clouds made of?
items.answer:  Clouds are visible masses composed of tiny water droplets, microscopic ice crystals, or a mixture of both, suspended high in the atmosphere.

items.stem: What causes floods in plains like Uttar Pradesh and Bihar during monsoons?
items.answer:  Heavy monsoon rainfall generates massive water runoff that rivers cannot carry away quickly, or the rivers themselves swell and overflow their banks, inundating the normally dry plains.

items.stem: Explain what a glacial burst is and why it occurs.
items.answer:  A glacial burst happens when a lake formed by melting glaciers, held back by ice or rock debris, breaks through its barrier due to excessive meltwater or heavy rain, causing devastating downstream floods.

items.stem: Why are cities sometimes prone to flooding during heavy rainfall?
items.answer:  Urban flooding occurs due to overburdened drainage systems, construction blocking waterways, and large areas of concrete/asphalt surfaces that prevent rainwater from soaking into the ground.

items.stem: What triggers landslides, and which regions in India are prone to them?
items.answer:  Landslides (collapse of rock/soil) are triggered by heavy rain, earthquakes, or volcanic activity. Hilly regions like the Himalayas (Himachal, Uttarakhand, Sikkim) and the Western Ghats are prone to them.

items.stem: List two causes of forest fires
items.answer:  Forest fires can be caused by dry climatic conditions (droughts), high winds spreading flames rapidly, or human carelessness (like unattended campfires or discarded cigarettes).

items.stem: What is the ‘greenhouse effect’, and why is it naturally important?
items.answer:  The greenhouse effect is the natural process where certain gases (CO2, etc.) in the atmosphere trap some of the sun’s heat, warming the Earth enough to support life.

items.stem: How have human activities intensified the greenhouse effect, leading to global warming?
items.answer:  Burning fossil fuels, deforestation, and industrial processes have released excessive amounts of greenhouse gases rapidly, trapping extra heat and causing the planet to warm unnaturally fast (global warming).

items.stem: What does climate ‘mitigation’ involve? Give one example.
items.answer:  Climate mitigation involves taking steps to slow down global warming and reduce its causes. Examples include cutting greenhouse gas emissions, planting trees, or switching to renewable energy sources. LONG ANSWER QUESTIO 

items.stem: Analyse the difference between the climate of Srinagar (North India) and Kanniyakumari (South India) using the factor of latitude.
items.answer:  Kanniyakumari, near the Equator (low latitude), receives direct solar radiation, resulting in a hot climate year-round. Srinagar, at a higher latitude, receives slanted solar rays spread over a larger area and passing through more atmosphere, leading to less heat and a much cooler climate with distinct seasons. NODIA CH 03: Climates of India

items.stem: Compare the annual temperature range of Mumbai (coastal) and Nagpur (inland), explaining the reason for the difference using the concept of proximity to the sea.
items.answer:  Mumbai, being coastal, has a smaller temperature range (approx. 14°C) because the sea moderates temperatures (cooler summers, milder winters). Nagpur, being inland and far from the sea’s influence, experiences extreme temperatures – very hot summers and colder winters – resulting in a much larger range (approx. 34°C).

items.stem: Analyse the role of the Western Ghats during the southwest monsoon. Why does the Deccan plateau east of the Ghats receive less rain?
items.answer:  The Western Ghats act as a barrier to the moisture-laden southwest monsoon winds coming from the Arabian Sea. The mountains force the winds to rise, cool, and release heavy rainfall on their western slopes. The Deccan plateau lies in the rain shadow area east of the Ghats, receiving significantly less rainfall as the winds descend and become drier.

items.stem: “The monsoon is a double-edged sword for India’s agriculture and economy.” Analyse this statement.
items.answer:  Monsoons are vital, bringing necessary rain for agriculture, filling rivers, and recharging groundwater, boosting the economy. However, ‘monsoon failure’ (less rain) causes drought and economic hardship, while excessive rain can cause devastating floods, destroying crops and infrastructure. Thus, its variability presents both benefits and risks.

items.stem: Explain how human activities like deforestation and improper construction can increase the risk or severity of landslides.
items.answer:  Deforestation removes tree roots that help bind soil together on slopes, making them unstable. Improper construction on hillsides, especially cutting into slopes or blocking natural water drainage, can further destabilize the land, increasing the likelihood and impact of landslides, particularly during heavy rains.

items.stem: Analyse the environmental and economic consequences of large-scale forest fires.
items.answer:  Environmentally, forest fires destroy vast habitats, kill wildlife, release large amounts of CO2 (contributing to climate change), degrade ecosystems, and worsen air quality. Economically, they destroy valuable timber resources, impact tourism, can damage property, displace communities, and require costly firefighting and restoration efforts.

items.stem: Explain the link between the burning of fossil fuels and global warming. Why is this a major concern?
items.answer:  Burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) releases large quantities of greenhouse gases, primarily CO2, into the atmosphere. These gases trap extra heat, enhancing the natural greenhouse effect and causing the Earth’s average temperature to rise rapidly (global warming). This is concerning because it disrupts established climate patterns globally.

items.stem: Analyse how climate change can lead to an increase in the frequency or intensity of climate- related disasters like floods or heat waves.
items.answer:  Global warming alters weather patterns. It can lead to more intense rainfall events (increasing flood risk), prolonged dry spells (increasing drought and fire risk), and more frequent and severe heat waves as average temperatures rise. Warmer oceans can also fuel more powerful cyclones.

items.stem: How can understanding climate patterns help communities prepare for natural disasters? Provide an example.
items.answer:  Knowing a region’s climate patterns (e.g., likelihood of cyclones on the east coast during a specific season, or flood risk during monsoon in certain river basins) allows communities and governments to develop early warning systems, build appropriate infrastructure (like cyclone shelters or flood barriers), and plan evacuation routes, reducing vulnerability. items.stem: Evaluate the role of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) in managing climate- related disasters in India.
items.answer:  The NDRF plays a crucial specialized role. Its trained personnel are deployed during disasters like cyclones, floods, and landslides for immediate rescue and evacuation operations. Their pre- positioning in vulnerable areas based on forecasts allows for rapid response, saving lives and providing critical initial relief, making them vital for disaster management.

items.stem: Compare the causes of flooding in Himalayan regions (glacial bursts) versus urban areas (poor drainage).
items.answer:  Himalayan floods can be caused by natural glacial lake outbursts due to rapid melting or excess rain overwhelming natural barriers. Urban flooding is often exacerbated by human factors : inadequate or blocked drainage systems unable to cope with heavy rain, and impermeable concrete surfaces preventing water absorption.

items.stem: Analyse the connection between climate, culture, and festivals in India, using an example like Baisakhi or Pongal.
items.answer:  India’s climate, particularly the monsoon and seasonal cycles, heavily influences agriculture. Many festivals are timed around harvest seasons, celebrating agricultural bounty. Baisakhi marks the spring harvest in North India, while Pongal celebrates the harvest in Tamil Nadu, reflecting the deep cultural integration of climate-dependent agriculture.

items.stem: Explain how a ‘microclimate’ like an ‘urban heat island’ forms and why it differs from the surrounding rural areas.
items.answer:  Urban heat islands form because cities replace vegetation with concrete and asphalt, which absorb and retain more solar heat. Waste heat from vehicles, buildings, and industry also contributes. Reduced vegetation limits cooling through evapotranspiration. This trapped heat makes cities significantly warmer than surrounding greener, rural areas.

items.stem: “Climate mitigation efforts often clash with the desire for economic growth.” Analyse why this conflict occurs.
items.answer:  Many mitigation measures (like reducing fossil fuel use, stricter environmental regulations) can be perceived as increasing costs for industries or slowing down development projects reliant on cheaper, polluting technologies. This creates a conflict between short-term economic gains and the long-term environmental necessity of addressing climate change.

items.stem: Considering India’s diverse climates, analyse why a single national policy might be difficult to implement for agriculture or water management.
items.answer:  India’s vast climatic diversity – from alpine cold to desert heat, heavy monsoon regions to semi-arid zones – means agricultural practices and water availability vary immensely. A policy suitable for the wet tropics (e.g., rice cultivation) would fail in arid Rajasthan. Therefore, region-specific strategies adapting to local climate realities are essential. CASE BASED QUESTIO 

items.stem: A travel company is planning tours for European tourists visiting India in December-January. They want to offer options covering different climate experiences. They are considering tours to Shimla (Himachal Pradesh), Jaipur (Rajasthan), and Goa (West Coast). Advise them on the likely climate/ weather in each location during that period. (i) Describe the likely climate/weather in Shimla during December-January. (ii) Describe the likely climate/weather in Jaipur during December-January. (iii) Describe the likely climate/weather in Goa during December-January.
items.answer:  (i) Shimla, a hill station with a temperate/alpine influence, will likely experience cold weather, possibly with freezing temperatures and snowfall, requiring heavy winter clothing. (ii) Jaipur, in the subtropical/semi-arid zone, will likely have pleasant days but cold nights NODIA CH 03: Climates of India and mornings. Winters are generally dry. Moderate warm clothing would be needed. (iii) Goa, on the coast with a tropical influence, will have mild and pleasant weather, neither too hot nor too cold, due to the moderating effect of the sea. Light clothing would suffice.

items.stem: Farmers in the Deccan Plateau (semi-arid climate) rely on monsoon rains for their crops like cotton and pulses. One year, the southwest monsoon is significantly delayed and rainfall is 40% below normal (‘monsoon failure’). Describe potential immediate consequences for the farmers and the local economy. (i) What is the primary impact of monsoon failure on crop cultivation in this region? (ii) How might this affect the availability and cost of food locally? (iii) Evaluate one socio-economic consequence for the farming community beyond crop loss.
items.answer:  (i) Lack of sufficient rain will lead to poor crop growth or even crop failure, drastically reducing the harvest of essential crops like cotton and pulses. (ii) Reduced harvest means less local food availability, leading to shortages and higher prices for essential food items like pulses in the local markets. (iii) Farmers might face severe financial distress due to lost income, potentially leading to debt. Agricultural labourers might lose work opportunities, forcing them to migrate to cities seeking alternative livelihoods.

items.stem: Following heavy monsoon rains, a village in the Western Ghats region experiences a landslide that blocks the main road and damages some houses on the lower slopes. The area was known for recent deforestation activity on the upper slopes for a new construction project. (i) Which two factors mentioned likely contributed to this landslide? (ii) Explain how deforestation might have increased the landslide risk. (iii) Suggest one preventive measure communities or authorities could take to reduce future landslide risk in such areas.
items.answer:  (i) Heavy monsoon rainfall and recent deforestation on the upper slopes are the two contributing factors mentioned. (ii) Tree roots help hold soil together on slopes. Removing trees through deforestation weakens the soil structure, making the slope unstable and more prone to collapse during heavy rains. (iii) Implementing strict regulations against deforestation on steep slopes and promoting afforestation (planting trees) can help stabilize the soil. Ensuring construction follows safe engineering practices that respect natural drainage is also crucial.

items.stem: A coastal city on India’s east coast receives an IMD alert for an approaching cyclone with very high wind speeds. The alert level is ‘Red (Take Action)’. The NDRF team is deployed. Describe the potential dangers and necessary actions. (i) What are the major dangers associated with a severe cyclone hitting the coast? (ii) What immediate action should residents in vulnerable low-lying coastal areas take upon receiving a ‘Red’ alert? (iii) What is the primary role of the NDRF in this situation?
items.answer:  (i) Dangers include extremely high winds damaging structures, heavy rainfall causing floods, storm surges (rising sea levels) inundating coastal areas, loss of life, and disruption of essential services. (ii) Residents should immediately evacuate to designated cyclone shelters or safer locations inland as instructed by authorities, securing their homes and belongings as much as possible beforehand. (iii) The NDRF’s primary role is to assist in evacuation efforts before the cyclone hits and conduct search and rescue operations immediately after the cyclone passes to save lives.

Scientists warn this contributes significantly to global warming and climate change, predicting more frequent droughts affecting the country’s agriculture in the long run. (iii) Suggest one ‘mitigation’ strategy the country could adopt to address this issue, considering both environment and economy.
items.answer:  (i) Coal is a fossil fuel primarily made of carbon. Burning it combines carbon with oxygen from the air, releasing large amounts of carbon dioxide (CO2) gas into the atmosphere. (ii) Increased CO2 traps more heat (enhanced greenhouse effect), raising global temperatures. This warming disrupts weather patterns, potentially leading to changes in rainfall distribution, including more frequent or severe droughts in some regions. (iii) The country could invest in transitioning towards renewable energy sources like solar or wind power.
